title: Summarize Cost Considerations Related to Cloud Usage

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud resources cost money differently depending on how they are purchased and how efficiently they are used.
CompTIA wants you to recognize cloud billing models and techniques that help organizations understand and control spending.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is the organization paying for exclusivity, committing ahead of time, paying only for current usage, accepting interruption for savings, or trying to control waste?
sections.callout: Workload predictability + usage pattern + cost requirement → choose the billing approach.

entries.title: Dedicated Host
paragraphs: A dedicated host provides physical host resources for one customer rather than sharing that host with unrelated tenants.
Because the customer receives dedicated physical capacity, it normally costs more than shared alternatives.
Think: Rent the whole building.
entries.recognitionCue: If physical host resources must be dedicated to one customer → think dedicated host.

entries.title: Reserved Resources
paragraphs: Reserved resources involve committing to resources ahead of time for a period of expected usage.
The customer may receive better pricing because the usage is predictable and committed.
Think: I know I'll need this for a while, so I'll commit now.
entries.recognitionCue: If a stable predictable workload can make a longer commitment for savings → think reserved resources.

entries.title: Pay-As-You-Go
paragraphs: With pay-as-you-go, the organization pays according to the resources it consumes instead of committing to a large amount of capacity in advance.
It provides flexibility for changing workloads.
Think: Use it → pay for it.
entries.recognitionCue: If usage changes and the organization wants flexibility without a long-term resource commitment → think pay-as-you-go.

entries.title: Spot Instance
paragraphs: A spot instance uses available excess cloud capacity at a reduced cost, with the tradeoff that the resource may be interrupted when the provider needs that capacity back.
Think: Cheap seat, but you may get kicked out.
This is best suited to workloads that can tolerate interruption.
entries.recognitionCue: If lowest compute price matters and the workload can survive interruption → think spot instance.

sections.title: Resource Metering
paragraphs: Resource metering measures how many cloud resources are being consumed.
Examples include compute usage, storage consumption, and network usage.
Metering helps providers calculate charges and customers understand where spending occurs.
Think: Cloud utility meter.
sections.callout: If the requirement is measuring cloud consumption → think resource metering.

sections.title: Tagging
paragraphs: Tagging attaches labels or metadata to cloud resources.
Tags can identify a department, project, application, environment, or owner.
From a cost perspective, tagging helps determine who or what is generating the expense.
Think: Put a name tag on the bill.
sections.callout: If costs need to be tracked by department, application, team, or project → think tagging.

sections.title: Rightsizing
paragraphs: Rightsizing adjusts resources so they better match actual workload requirements.
A virtual machine with far more CPU and memory than it ever uses may be wasting money.
A smaller appropriately sized resource could meet the same requirement at lower cost.
Think: Not too big. Not too small. Just right.
sections.callout: If resources are consistently underused and cost must decrease → think rightsizing.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Exclusive physical cloud host → Dedicated host
Predictable workload and commitment → Reserved resources
Variable workload with no commitment → Pay-as-you-go
Interruptible workload seeking low cost → Spot instance
Attribute charges by project or team → Tagging
Resource bigger than the workload requires → Rightsizing

entries.title: Reserved Resources vs. Pay-As-You-Go
paragraphs: Reserved resources point to predictable usage and commitment. Pay-as-you-go points to flexibility and consumption-based usage.

entries.title: Spot Instance vs. Pay-As-You-Go
paragraphs: Both avoid the same kind of long commitment associated with reservations, but spot resources have one key clue: interruption is acceptable.

entries.title: Resource Metering vs. Tagging
paragraphs: Metering tells you how much was consumed. Tagging helps tell you who or what the resource belongs to.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Need exclusive physical host → Dedicated host
Interruptible job with the lowest price → Spot instance
Identify which department owns a cost → Tagging
